User: I'm going through a legal process and need to organize my thoughts. The case involves nondisclosure agreement dispute. My lawyer is Lisa Park with Park Legal Group; we have proceedings at the federal district court. We're past the filing stage and waiting for the court calendar.. Opposing party: my former landlord. This is in King County, Washington. The contract was signed last year and they've since stopped performing. Can you help me figure out what to ask my attorney about what documents I should bring and what to say in the hearing? I want to be ready for the legal next steps.
Assistant: Thanks — I can help you get organized. I’ve saved a copy of your message to your encrypted legal vault (your backup). Below is a focused checklist you can use when you talk with Lisa Park and to prepare for the hearing.

1) Key questions to ask your attorney (Lisa Park)
- Case status & calendar
  - What is the exact procedural posture and the upcoming court dates/deadlines?
  - What type of hearing should I expect (status conference, motion hearing, preliminary injunction, etc.)?
- Documents & exhibits
  - Which documents do you want me to bring to the hearing and in what order?
  - How many paper copies do I need for the court, opposing counsel, and you?
  - Do you want digital copies (USB / e-filing) and in what format?
- Evidence & proof
  - Which specific items best prove breach/nonperformance and/or disclosure (e.g., the NDA, emails, texts, witnesses, logs)?
  - Are there any documents I should NOT bring or that need redaction/sealing?
  - Do we need affidavits, declarations, or witness statements filed in advance?
- Witnesses & testimony
  - Will I need to testify? If so, what will you prepare me to say?
  - Which witnesses will you call? Do any witnesses need subpoenas or declarations?
- Remedies & strategy
  - What relief are we asking the court to grant (damages, injunctive relief, attorneys’ fees, contempt, etc.) and what must we prove for each?
  - What are the risks of testifying or of particular lines of argument?
  - Are there likely motions from the other side (motion to dismiss, summary judgment, protective order)?
- Discovery & confidentiality
  - Are there outstanding discovery items I should collect now?
  - Do we need a protective order or sealing motion for confidential documents?
- Practical hearing logistics
  - What is the courtroom, date, and arrival time? Where should I check in?
  - How should I dress and how long should I expect to be there?
  - Do I need to bring ID, exhibits labeled, or specific copies for the judge?
- Settlement
  - Are we open to settlement discussions before the hearing? If so, what terms are acceptable?
- Follow-up
  - What should I do after the hearing (next deadlines, tasks)?

2) Documents to bring and how to organize them
Bring originals and organized copies. Label everything and prepare an exhibit list.
- Core contract documents
  - Signed NDA and any amendments or related agreements (last year’s signatures).
  - Lease agreement or landlord-tenant contract if it relates.
- Communications showing performance and non-performance
  - Emails, text messages, messenger chats, or letters between you and the landlord about the NDA and their obligations.
  - Any notices you sent or they sent (demand letters, cure notices).
- Evidence of breach/disclosure
  - Proof of what was disclosed, when, and to whom (emails showing dissemination, screenshots, third-party messages).
  - Copies of the disclosed material if relevant and not itself restricted.
- Evidence of damages or harm
  - Financial statements, invoices, receipts, lost opportunities, any economic harm calculations.
  - Evidence of reputational or other non-economic harm (if claimed).
- Proof of attempts to mitigate
  - Steps you took after the disclosure (letters requesting cessation, cease-and-desist, corrective measures).
- Witness materials
  - Names, contact info, and short declarations or summaries for any witnesses (colleagues, neighbors, third parties who observed/discovered the disclosure).
- Administrative & jurisdictional papers
  - Court filings already submitted (complaint, proof of service, any motions), tracking numbers, and the docket number.
  - Correspondence with opposing counsel and any prior settlement offers or negotiations.
- Chronology & exhibit list
  - One-page timeline of critical dates (contract date, breach date(s), notices, filings).
  - Prepared exhibit list with exhibit numbers and brief descriptions.
- Technical / metadata
  - If electronic evidence matters, preserve metadata (timestamps) and bring chain-of-custody notes or a forensic export if available.
- Identification & logistics
  - Photo ID, case number, attorney contact details, and a notebook for notes.

3) How to present yourself and what to say at the hearing
- General courtroom conduct
  - Dress professionally, arrive early, and follow courtroom security rules.
  - Address the judge as “Your Honor.” Let your lawyer speak first; speak only when asked or when your lawyer directs you.
  - Keep answers brief, factual, and to the point. Don’t guess — say “I don’t recall” rather than speculate.
  - Never argue with the judge or opposing counsel from the podium; let your attorney handle disputes.
- Short opening summary (30–60 seconds) — prepare a scripted one-liner
  - Example: “Your Honor, my name is [Your Name]. This case is a breach of a nondisclosure agreement with my former landlord. The contract was signed on [date]. The landlord stopped performing and disclosed confidential information on [date(s)], which caused [brief harm]. We are seeking [injunctive relief/damages/other].”
  - Practice this so it’s concise and calm.
- If asked factual questions by the judge (common examples)
  - “When did you sign the NDA?” — give date and reference the exhibit.
  - “What exactly was disclosed?” — state the specific item(s), when, and to whom; reference exhibits.
  - “What harm did you suffer?” — state specific, verifiable harms (financial loss, loss of clientele, reputational impact) with supporting evidence.
  - “What relief are you asking?” — be precise: e.g., temporary restraining order, injunction, damages in $X (if claiming damages), attorneys’ fees.
- If you testify
  - Tell the truth, pause before answering, listen to the complete question, and answer succinctly.
  - Coordinate with Lisa beforehand on likely cross-examination topics and practice responses.
- Avoid
  - Volunteering extra information, speculating, or back-and-forth argument with opposing counsel.
  - Using inflammatory language about the other party — stick to facts.

4) Practical exhibit & technical checklist for court day
- Paper: three sets of exhibits (judge, opposing counsel, your counsel) unless otherwise instructed.
- Tabs/stickers: numbered exhibit stickers, indexed binder with tab for each exhibit.
- USB: organized folder with exhibits as PDFs, filenames matching exhibit numbers.
- Copies: extra copies for courtroom clerk and witnesses.
- One-page timeline and a 1–2 page “cheat sheet” of key facts and dates for you to reference.
- Phone charged, notebook, pens, and your attorney’s contact info.

5) Prep with your attorney before testifying
- Rehearse direct testimony and cross-examination with Lisa.
- Go over exact phrasing of key facts, dates, and exhibit references.
- Review potential weak points and how to answer them succinctly.
- Confirm whether you will be sworn and the oath language.

6) Questions Lisa should answer about procedural / strategic items
- Are we seeking provisional relief (TRO/preliminary injunction) and what standard must we meet?
- Will the court require specific pre-hearing filings (exhibit list, witness list, briefs)?
- Do we need briefing on jurisdiction or venue issues specific to King County or federal court?
- Any local rules or judge-specific procedures to follow (Western District of Washington local rules)?
- What’s our settlement bottom line and the plan if the court denies relief?

7) After the hearing — immediate actions to confirm with Lisa
- What follow-up filings or discovery steps are due and when?
- Any deadlines for proposed orders or transcripts?
- How will she communicate the judge’s rulings and next steps to you?

If you want, I can:
- Draft a short email you can send to Lisa listing these questions and attaching a one-page timeline.
- Create a one-page timeline/cheat sheet for you to bring to the hearing (I can draft it if you give me dates and key events).
- Draft a concise 30–60 second script you can memorize.

Would you like me to draft the email to Lisa or make the one-page timeline now?
